newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Anti-U.S. feeling aired at Mobutu party rally.
newsitem.headline: Anti-U.S. feeling aired at Mobutu party rally.

text.p: Mobutu Sese Seko's remaining loyalists staged a show of support for Zaire's sick president on Sunday, accusing the United States of sponsoring the rebels who control more than half the country.
About 3,000 members of Mobutu's Popular Revolutionary Movement (MPR) turned out in the capital Kinshasa, which rebel leader Laurent Kabila says he will capture by June.
The MPR's acting leader, Mananga Dintoka Pholo, said Kabila had the blessing of a "Western power" when he launched his rebellion in the east last October with the help of Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.
Mananga reiterated the government's disgust that a U.S. company, America Mining Fields (AMF), signed what it said was a $1 billion mining contract with the rebels this month.
AMF is registered in Canada but has its headquarters in President Bill Clinton's home town of Hope, Arkansas.
"The principal of the allies is to seize our mineral riches," Mananga said to applause.
In his speech at the People's Palace, Mananga did not mention the United States by name but there was no doubt which power MPR supporters blame.
"Kabila has the support of the Americans but not of the people," said Jose Leda, a student aged 31.
"Even if Kabila wins remember we are Africans with the magic to make sure Clinton dies before Mobutu," Leda, from the same Equateur region as Mobutu, added.
"The Americans have eaten with Mobutu all these years and now they are trying to get rid of him," said Kalambayi Wetu, from rebel-held Eastern Kasai province.

The 66-year-old president did not attend the meeting of the once-omnipotent party he founded in 1967 and whose 30th birthday party on May 20 could be spoiled by the rebels. Mobutu remains cloistered in his residence inside a Kinshasa barracks, receiving few visitors.
He is battling prostate cancer as well as the coalition of enemies who have routed his army and are poised to end his 32-year rule.
The increasing anti-West and anti-U.S. rhetoric emanating from the beleaguered regime coincides with the imminent arrival of Bill Richardson, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations.

A U.S. embassy spokesman said Richardson would arrive in Kinshasa "in principle" on Monday. A task force of U.S., Belgian, British and French troops is across the river from Kinshasa, in the Congolese capital Brazzaville, ready to move in to evacuate their nationals if violence erupts.
Diplomats in New York said earlier Richardson would try to get peace negotiations started between Mobutu and Kabila.
The two old foes have both agreed to meet but a neutral venue is one problem and Kabila's insistence that the only item on the agenda is Mobutu's departure is another.
The sense that the rebels are closing in pervades the atmosphere in Kinshasa, an unkempt city of five million people.
The rebels are still at least 400 km (250 miles) away in the east but could threaten the capital much faster if Angola allows them to cross its territory and seize Zaire's only seaport at Matadi.
Zaire said on Friday 1,400 Angola troops had invaded from the enclave of Cabinda and moved into the border town of Yema.
On Sunday state radio claimed two Angolan army helicopters landed on Friday evening at Kimpangu and Kimvula, inside Zaire, less than 200 km (125 miles) due south of the capital.

Angola has denied such claims but expatriate mining officials in Angola said on Friday the Zairean rebels and the Angolan army were performing joint military exercises at Dundo, on the Angolan side of the border.
Mobutu's long-term support for Angola's UNITA rebels would explain the government's help for Kabila, diplomats in Kinshasa said.
